content.text: How did the universe begin? The Big Bang theory is the prevailing scientific explanation for the origin of the universe. It describes how the universe expanded from an incredibly hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago. Understanding this theory helps us make sense of the universe's structure, composition, and ongoing evolution.

The Big Bang theory states that the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since. It is supported by multiple independent lines of evidence.
What is the Big Bang Theory?
The universe began in an extremely hot, dense state
It has been expanding and cooling ever since
Space, time, and all matter/energy originated in this event
What the Big Bang Was NOT
NOT an explosion into pre-existing space
NOT an explosion at a point in space
Space itself was created and expanded
The Big Bang happened everywhere—all points were at the origin

items.description: Light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths, showing they are moving away. More distant galaxies recede faster, indicating the universe is expanding from a common origin.

items.description: Uniform microwave radiation detected from all directions at 2.7 K. This is the cooled afterglow of the hot, dense early universe, red shifted from gamma rays to microwaves.

Predicted by Big Bang theory before discovery

items.title: Abundance of Light Elements
items.description: The universe is approximately 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with small amounts of lithium. This ratio matches predictions for nuclear reactions in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
bullets: Too much helium for stars alone to have created
Ratio is consistent everywhere in the universe

"The Big Bang happened at a point"
— All of space was concentrated; there was no "outside."

— "Before" may not be meaningful, as time itself began with the Big Bang.
"The Big Bang is just a theory"

The four key pieces of evidence for the Big Bang are: (1) red shift of galaxies, (2) cosmic microwave background radiation, (3) abundance of light elements, and (4) evolution of galaxies over cosmic time.
Big Bang: universe began hot and dense ~13.8 billion years ago
Cosmic microwave background (afterglow of hot early universe)
Abundance of hydrogen/helium (formed in first minutes)
Evolution of galaxies over cosmic time

The CMB is low-intensity microwave radiation coming uniformly from all directions in space at a temperature of 2.725 K. It supports the Big Bang because the theory predicts the early universe was extremely hot and dense. About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe cooled enough for atoms to form, releasing radiation. The expansion of space has since stretched this radiation from gamma rays to microwaves. Its discovery confirmed a key prediction of Big Bang theory.

The CMB was originally emitted as high-energy gamma radiation when the universe was about 3000 K. Since then, the universe has expanded by a factor of about 1000, stretching the wavelength of this radiation by the same factor. This red shift has moved it from the gamma/visible range into the microwave range.

The red shift of galaxies tells us that the universe is expanding. Distant galaxies are all moving away from us, with more distant galaxies receding faster (Hubble's law). This implies that in the past, all matter was closer together, supporting the Big Bang origin of the universe.
— space itself is stretching, not galaxies moving through space (explanation)

An explosion occurs at a point in pre-existing space and expands outward into surrounding space. The Big Bang was not like this. Space itself was created in the Big Bang and has been expanding ever since. There is no centre and no edge — the expansion happens everywhere uniformly. Every point in the universe was at the origin.
— the balloon analogy helps illustrate this (explanation)

The age is determined by (i) measuring the Hubble constant H₀ and extrapolating backward — if expansion rate is known, we can estimate when all matter was at one point (age ≈ 1/H₀); (ii) detailed analysis of the CMB fluctuation patterns gives a precise value of 13.8 ± 0.02 billion years; (iii) this is consistent with the ages of the oldest known stars in globular clusters (~12-13 billion years).

At time zero, the universe was infinitely hot and dense (singularity). Within the first second, fundamental particles (quarks, electrons) formed as the universe expanded and cooled rapidly. By about 10⁻⁶ seconds, quarks combined to form protons and neutrons. By about 3 minutes, the temperature had fallen to about 10⁹ K, allowing nucleosynthesis: protons and neutrons fused to form hydrogen, helium, and small amounts of lithium nuclei.
— this explains the observed 75% H / 25% He ratio (recall + explanation)
